newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan parties formally decide on MOF reform plan.
newsitem.headline: Japan parties formally decide on MOF reform plan.

text.p: The three parties in Japan's loose ruling alliance formally agreed on Wednesday to a plan to reform the powerful Finance Ministry and strip it of its role of inspecting and supervising financial institutions, according a statement obtained by Reuters.

The statement said the three parties expect the government to submit relevant legislation to the next regular session of parliament in late January and to implement the reforms in the fiscal year starting in April 1998.
The main points of the agreement are as follows:

-- ministry's banking and securities bureaux would merge and take over some of the functions of the international finance bureau. The international finance bureau would retain its basic system for the time being.
-- A fully independent body would be established under the Prime Minister's Office to take over the ministry's functions of inspecting and supervising financial institutions.
-- The new body would be tentatively named the Financial Inspection and Supervision Agency.

-- The head of the agency would be appointed by the prime minister and would have the right to appoint agency employees. The independence of the head of the agency and the employees must be strictly enforced.

-- The new body would oversee all financial institutions -- banks, agricultural financial firms, non-bank financial firms and labour credit associations -- which are are now supervised by different ministries. But the inspection and supervisory functions of this body will be shared by the Agriculture Ministry, the Labour Ministry and the Trade Ministry, which currently oversee relevant financial institutions.
-- The new body must hold regular meetings with the Finance Ministry to discuss financial matters from the viewpoint of maintaining Japan's credit order.

-- The new agency would be responsible for handling financial failures but would be expected to consult with the finance minister on any failures that could not be handled within the current framework of procedures. Severe crises would be dealt with by the cabinet and the agency.
-- The new agency would have jurisdiction over Japan's Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission.
-- The ministry's regional bureaux would retain a role in the inspection and supervision of regional financial institutions.
-- The three parties will continue discussions on how Japan's deposit insurance system should be reformed.

-- The issue of separating fiscal policy from the ministry will be discussed in Japan's overall administrative reforms. Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashomoto has vowed to complete administrative reforms by 2001.
